newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE- Is Taiwan's dollar overvalued?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE- Is Taiwan's dollar overvalued?.

text.p: Is the time now ripe for a Taiwan dollar devaluation?

During three months of trading doldrums, many currency dealers and market analysts said they felt the currency should weaken to reflect Taiwan's sluggish economic recovery and flagging competitiveness in the world market.

Until a panicky but relatively minor downturn on October 22-23 pushed the Taiwan dollar briefly below T$27.6 to the U.S. dollar, the Taiwanese currency had idled between T$27.47 and T$27.52 since August -- a level apparently satisfactory to what has been a lavishly indulgent central bank.

The central bank spent an estimated US$10 billion to defend the currency at T$27.5 during months of alarming war games and missile tests mounted by China in the run-up to Taiwan's historic presidential election in March.

But Chen Yen-pao of the Chung-hua Institution for Economic Research, a Taipei think tank, said the slow return of capital that fled during the crisis and an anaemic recovery suggested the currency would serve Taiwan better at T$27.7 to T$27.8.
"Simply put, the Taiwan dollar is slightly overvalued," Chen said in an interview, emphasising that he spoke for himself, not his institution.
Taiwan, hailed in the 1970s and 1980s as an export-spewing "Asian dragon", is grappling with structural changes that come with a maturing economy and a pluralistic, consumer society.
FACTORS WHICH HURT INVESTMENT CLIMATE

Rising labour costs, environmental concerns and a boisterous, but often-paralysed, parliament have combined to hurt the island's investment climate, ChinaTrust Commercial Bank chief economist Daniel Chen said.
"Taiwan's slipping on the competitive front does not bode well for the currency's long-term strength," Chen said.

Convertible in the current account, Taiwan's dollar remains subject to capital-account restrictions as the government knows looser controls could make Taiwan vulnerable by increasing its exposure to China's attractive but volatile economy.

The central bank won praise in May by trying to engineer a devaluation, saying it was abandoning its decade-old T$27.5 defence to stimulate exports. That sent the dollar sliding to within a few cents of T$28 in June, but recent months have seen it bounce back to precisely the old defence level.
Recent comments from central bank officials indicate a devaluation is no longer a priority.

Vice-governor Liang Cheng-chin attributed the late-October decline to "false expectations" of a depreciation, saying that Taiwan's sluggish economy was showing signs of recovering and that the U.S. dollar had not shown strength that would warrant pushing the Taiwan dollar lower.

Liang said that local deposit interest rates were not overly low in comparison to other countries and that fears of investors switching Taiwan dollar holdings to foreign exchange in a quest for higher returns were unjustified.
FOREIGN FUNDS HELP IN PART

Partially offsetting the capital flight is a persistent influx of foreign funds lured by Taiwan's liberalising financial markets. About half of the US$20 billion approved to date for stock market investment has been exchanged into Taiwan dollars.
"Without the foreign funds, the Taiwan dollar would have been weaker," a foreign bank dealer said.
But the handsome flow of foreign funds is far from making up for Taiwan's huge capital outflow, ChinaTrust's Chen said.
"Over time, Taiwan's once-enviable current account surplus will deteriorate. And the currency should reflect it," he said.

No accurate figures are available, but a manager at a Taiwan bank's offshore banking unit cited estimates that US$15 billion of the capital that fled Taiwan since ties with China soured in mid-1995 had stayed overseas -- about 70 percent of the total.
"And the drain is continuing," he noted, asking that his name not be used.

The bank manager said Taiwan people seeking immigrant visas for New Zealand bought as much as NZ$10 billion in the year from July 1995. He said capital a exodus to Canada, Australia and other emigrant destinations followed a similar pattern.
Expecting a weaker Taiwan dollar, exporters are slow to repatriate profits, which has resulted in about US$3 billion sitting in foreign currency accounts, currency dealers said.
Relatively weak local consumption has forced importers to scale back demand for foreign exchange, they said.
Even as macroeconomic factors slowly work their way into currency valuation, the Taiwan dollar's level remains determined to a strong degree by policy considerations.

In the opening up of Taiwan's financial markets, financial authorities have tried to keep volatility out of the currency, Morris Li, vice president and treasurer of Citibank's emerging markets group in Taipei, said.
Foreign investors are encouraged to invest in Taiwan stocks and bonds while resting assured that there is little currency risk involved.
"I don't think the Taiwan dollar will be allowed to become a speculative vehicle like the Thai baht," Li said. "Taiwan is modelling after Singapore on keeping a stable currency."
